218.title: Let the children come (Mark 10:1–16)
218.hook: the disciples shoo the children, and he is indignant
218.howItsDone: The Catholic Church baptizes infants, and parishes often bless children at Mass who are too young to receive Communion; Mark 10:13–16 is among the passages read at infant baptisms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child in the middle, while the disciples argued about who was greatest. Your line was last of all. Where did you go last? Today, more children, and the disciples still haven't learned. Day two hundred eighteen.

Picture an important person visiting a town, and the security detail keeping the crowds back. Now picture the kids trying to get through. Jesus has crossed into Judea, on the far side of the Jordan, heading south toward Jerusalem. Crowds again. Teachers come with a hard question about marriage. And in the middle of all this serious business, parents start bringing their children to him, so he'll touch them. The disciples step in and scold the parents. He's busy. Not now. And for the only time in Mark, we're told Jesus was indignant.
screen: `KEEPING THE KIDS BACK.` → `ON THE ROAD TO JERUSALEM.` → `THE DISCIPLES SCOLD THE PARENTS.`

segments.voice: First, the question before it. Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife. Jesus goes back past the Law to the beginning, to Genesis: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh. What God has joined, no one should separate. Catholics hear in these verses the root of the Church's teaching that a sacramental marriage is for life. Other Christians read the passage in other ways, and it's a tender subject in many families. Mark gives it in a few lines and moves on. Second, the scolding. The disciples rebuke the people bringing children. Maybe they're protecting him. Maybe kids just weren't important enough. Either way, they've forgotten yesterday already. Third, his anger. Mark's word is strong: indignant, much displeased. It's the only time Mark says it of Jesus. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer here is old English for allow. Let them come. Then he goes further: whoever doesn't receive the kingdom of God like a little child won't enter it. Not like a grown-up earning it. Like a child being handed it. Fourth, what he does. "And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them." Arms around them, hands on their heads, a blessing. This line is one reason the Church has long welcomed children, and one of the passages Catholics point to when they baptize infants, who can't earn anything, and simply receive.
screen: `FIRST, A QUESTION ABOUT MARRIAGE.` · `THE DISCIPLES SCOLD THE PARENTS.` · `INDIGNANT: LET THEM COME.` · `EMBRACED, TOUCHED, BLESSED.` · then, large: `OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive something like a child. Settle and breathe. A child doesn't earn a hug or a meal. They just open their hands. So open yours, palms up, on your lap. Now think of something good you've been handed lately and never quite received. A compliment you brushed off. Help you felt you had to pay back. Love you didn't think you'd earned. Let it land. Say thank you, out loud or inside. If you pray, you can receive it as a gift from God. The bell holds the time.
Let the children come. What Jesus says, indignant, when his disciples try to shoo the children away. Then he embraces and blesses them. Today's word.
Your line: of such is the kingdom. Today, the next time someone offers you something, don't argue or explain. Just say thank you and take it. Day two hundred eighteen.

219.title: Looking on him, loved him (Mark 10:17–31)
219.hook: the rich young man asks, Jesus loves him, and he goes away sad
219.howItsDone: Catholic religious brothers and sisters take a vow of poverty, following this invitation literally, while lay Catholics are taught to practice detachment and generosity, often through almsgiving, especially in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, let the children come: Jesus was indignant when they were sent away. Your line was of such is the kingdom. What did you receive without arguing? Today, a grown man who wants to earn it. Day two hundred nineteen.

Jesus is setting out on the road again when a man comes running up and drops to his knees in the dust. Running. Kneeling. This is someone who really wants an answer. He asks the biggest question there is: good master, what must I do to receive eternal life? He's done everything right. He's kept the commandments since he was a boy. He's not a villain in this story. He's the kind of person any parish would love to have. And what happens in the next few seconds is one of the saddest scenes in the Gospels, and also one of the tenderest.
screen: `A MAN RUNS UP AND KNEELS.` → `WHAT MUST I DO?` → `HE'S DONE EVERYTHING RIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the look. Jesus lists the commandments, and the man says he's kept them all from his youth. Then Mark adds five words no other Gospel has. In the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus looking on him, loved him." Before the hard part, before any test, Jesus looks at him and loves him. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and neither of them keeps that line. Mark does. Second, the one thing. "One thing is wanting unto thee: go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." It's the same invitation the fishermen got. Come, follow me. The hard words come from love, not from a trap. Third, the face. Mark says his face fell, and he went away sorrowful, "for he had great possessions." Not angry. Sad. He wanted it, and he couldn't let go. And Mark never tells us whether he came back. The sources are silent. By the way, only Matthew calls him young, and only Luke calls him a ruler. The rich young ruler is all three Gospels folded together. Fourth, the camel. Jesus says it's easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are stunned: then who can be saved? He looks at them too, and says: "With men it is impossible; but not with God." Catholics remember that around the year 270, a young Egyptian named Anthony heard this story read at church, gave his land away, and went into the desert. Most are not called to sell everything. All are called to be looked on, and loved, first.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away one thing you're attached to. Start by sitting still and breathing. Imagine being looked at, the way the man was: not inspected, loved. Stay in that for a minute. Then think of one thing you own that you hold a little too tightly. A jacket, a book, a gadget, a sum of money. Not everything. One thing. Picture who might need it. Decide to give it this week. If you pray, you can ask for open hands. The bell holds the time.
Looking on him. The five words only Mark keeps: Jesus looked at the rich man and loved him, before he asked anything hard. Today's word.
Your line: he loved him first. Today, before you ask anything hard of someone, look at them for a moment and find one thing to love. Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: Bartimaeus (Mark 10:32–52)
220.hook: a blind beggar shouts louder when told to be quiet, and is asked what do you want
220.tomorrow: the fig tree and the temple
220.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray short cries for mercy drawn from this Gospel, such as the Jesus Prayer, often repeated slowly with the breath or on a prayer rope or rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking on him: Jesus loved the rich man first, and the man went away sad. Your line was he loved him first. Who did you look at with love before asking? Today, a man who won't go away. Day two hundred twenty.

Everyone knows someone who won't take no for an answer. Today, that person is the hero. Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem now, walking out in front, and his followers are amazed and afraid. He tells them a third time what will happen there. Then they pass through Jericho, the last town before the climb to the city. A big crowd. And sitting by the side of the road, begging, is a blind man named Bartimaeus. He hears it's Jesus of Nazareth passing by. And he starts to shout.
screen: `WON'T TAKE NO FOR AN ANSWER.` → `JERICHO, THE LAST TOWN.` → `A BLIND MAN BEGINS TO SHOUT.`

segments.voice: First, the question before him. Just before Jericho, James and John come to Jesus and ask for a favor, and he asks them: what do you want me to do for you? They want the seats of honor, at his right and his left, in his glory. He tells them the Son of man "is not come to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a redemption for many." Hold on to that question. Second, the shout. Bartimaeus cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus son of David, have mercy on me." Son of David is a royal title, a king's name. The crowd tells him to be quiet. He shouts even louder. Third, the call. Jesus stops. He says, call him. And suddenly the same crowd is kind: "Be of better comfort: arise, he calleth thee." Bartimaeus throws off his cloak, maybe the only thing he owns, the one he spread out for coins, and jumps up. Remember yesterday's rich man, who couldn't let go of his possessions. Fourth, the same question again. "What wilt thou that I should do to thee?" Word for word, nearly, what he asked James and John. They asked for glory. Bartimaeus says: "Rabboni, that I may see." Jesus tells him his faith has made him whole, and he sees, and Mark says he followed him on the way. Bartimaeus is one of the only people healed in Mark who's named. Many think that's because the first readers knew him. His cry, have mercy on me, is part of the root of the Jesus Prayer that Eastern Christians, and many Catholics, pray to this day.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer what do you want. Settle and breathe. Imagine Jesus stopping on the road, turning, and asking you the question he asked Bartimaeus. What wilt thou that I should do to thee? Don't answer with what you think you're supposed to want. Answer with what you actually want. One sentence. It might be small. It might be enormous. Say it quietly. If you pray, you can say it to him as your prayer. If you don't, just notice what came up, and how it felt to name it. The bell holds the time.
Bartimaeus. The blind beggar at Jericho who shouted louder when told to be quiet, threw off his cloak, and followed. Today's word.
Your line: what wilt thou. Today, ask one person what they actually want from you, and then listen, the way Jesus stopped on the road. Day two hundred twenty.

221.title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:1–25)
221.word: The fig tree and the temple
221.hook: the king on a donkey, a withered tree, and pray believing and forgive
221.howItsDone: Catholics reenact the entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday with blessed palms and a procession, sing Hosanna in the Sanctus at every Mass, and exchange a sign of peace before Communion as a gesture of reconciliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartimaeus shouted louder, threw off his cloak, and followed Jesus on the way. Your line was what wilt thou. Who did you ask? The way he followed ends today, at the gates of Jerusalem. Day two hundred twenty-one.

Every Palm Sunday, Catholics walk into church waving palm branches, and a lot of kids think it's the fun Sunday. It starts here. Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey, a colt nobody has ever ridden. He rides it down into Jerusalem. People throw their cloaks on the road, and cut branches from the fields, and shout. It looks like a king arriving. Then, over the next day, he does two very strange things. He curses a fig tree. And he turns over tables in the Temple. Mark tells them woven together, on purpose.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY STARTS HERE.` → `A KING ON A YOUNG DONKEY.` → `A FIG TREE, AND THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: First, the shout. The crowd cries, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna, blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." Hosanna comes from Hebrew, save us, please. It's a line from the psalms, and Catholics still sing it at every Mass, just before the Eucharistic prayer's great moment. A king, but on a donkey, not a war horse. Second, the fig tree. The next morning he's hungry, sees a fig tree in leaf, and finds nothing but leaves. Mark adds, strangely, that it wasn't the season for figs. Jesus says no one will eat fruit from it again. Third, the Temple. He walks into the Temple courts and drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, and says: "My house shall be called the house of prayer to all nations? But you have made it a den of thieves." He's quoting two prophets, Isaiah and Jeremiah. The next morning they pass the fig tree, and it's withered from the roots. This is a Mark sandwich: tree, Temple, tree. Many readers hear the tree as a sign, the way prophets acted out signs: all leaves, no fruit. Busy worship that forgets to pray. Fourth, what Jesus says about it all. Not a lesson in cursing. A lesson in prayer. Have faith in God, he says: whatever you ask in prayer, believe. And then, the line that ends today's reading: "when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man; that your Father also, who is in heaven, may forgive you your sins." The house of prayer starts inside. Before you ask, let go.
screen: `HOSANNA: SAVE US, PLEASE.` · `LEAVES, AND NO FRUIT.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `WHEN YOU STAND TO PRAY, FORGIVE.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive before you pray. Settle and breathe. Let one face come to mind, someone you're holding something against. Not the biggest wound you have; start smaller. Picture them. Notice what your body does. Then, if you can, loosen your grip, even a little. Forgiving doesn't mean saying it was fine. It means not carrying it into this moment. If you pray, after that, bring whatever you were going to ask. If you don't, just let the space it left be quiet. The bell holds the time.
The fig tree and the temple. A tree with only leaves, a house of prayer turned into a market, and a lesson that ends: forgive when you pray. Today's word.
screen: `THE FIG TREE AND THE TEMPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: forgive, then pray. Today, before any prayer or any big ask of anyone, check whether you're holding something against someone, and set it down first. Day two hundred twenty-one.

222.title: Render to Caesar (Mark 11:27–12:17)
222.hook: a coin with Caesar's image; what bears God's image belongs to God
222.howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that citizens have duties to the state, such as paying taxes and voting, and that every human being is made in the image of God, which grounds its teaching on human dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fig tree and the temple: all leaves, no fruit, and a lesson that ended in forgiveness. Your line was forgive, then pray. What did you set down first? Today, Jesus is back in the Temple, and they've come to trap him. Day two hundred twenty-two.

You know the question that has no safe answer. The one at a family dinner that's really a trap: whichever way you answer, somebody's furious. Jesus walks the Temple courts, and the questions start. By what authority do you do these things? He answers with a question of his own, and tells a story about tenants who kill the owner's son. Then a group arrives with the perfect trap. Some are Pharisees. Some are supporters of Herod. They flatter him first. Then they ask: should we pay taxes to Caesar, or not?
screen: `A QUESTION WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.` → `BY WHAT AUTHORITY?` → `PAY TAXES TO CAESAR, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: First, the trap. If he says yes, pay, he sides with Rome, the occupier, and the crowd turns on him. If he says no, don't pay, he's a rebel, and Rome has a cross for rebels. There's no safe answer. Second, the coin. He says, bring me a penny, let me see it. The coin is a Roman denarius, the tax coin. And he asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whose is this image and inscription?" They say: Caesar's. The emperor's face is on it, and around the edge, words calling him the son of a god. Notice: he has to ask them for one, and they can produce it, there in the Temple courts. Third, the answer: render "to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." Mark says they marveled at him. It's not a dodge. It's an answer with a hook in it. The coin has Caesar's image, so it belongs to him; give it back. Then what has God's image on it? Anyone who knew the first page of Genesis would hear it. In the Douay-Rheims: "And God created man to his own image: to the image of God he created him." Early Christian writers loved this: the coin carries Caesar's face, and you carry God's. Fourth, what this means for Catholics now. The Church teaches that Christians owe real duties to their country: pay taxes, vote, serve the common good. But the state doesn't own the whole person. The deepest part, the image, belongs to God. So the line both honors earthly duty and sets a limit on it. Your wallet can go to Caesar. You can't.
screen: `A TRAP WITH NO SAFE ANSWER.` · `WHOSE IMAGE IS ON THE COIN?` · `GIVE CAESAR HIS COIN.` · `YOU CARRY GOD'S IMAGE.` · then, large: `AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your own face in a mirror. If there's one nearby, or your phone's camera, look now. If not, picture your face. Resist the usual checklist: hair, skin, tired eyes. Just look, the way you'd look at a coin to see whose image it bears. Catholics say that face was made in the image of God. Stay with that for a while. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let yourself be looked at kindly, even by yourself. The bell holds the time.
Render to Caesar. Give back to Caesar the coin with his face on it, and to God what bears God's image. Today's word.
Your line: you bear his image. Today, when you see a face, a stranger's, an annoying one, your own, remember whose image it's said to carry. Day two hundred twenty-two.

223.title: The widow's two mites (Mark 12:18–44)
223.hook: the great commandment, then a widow gives everything she has
223.howItsDone: Catholics give at the offertory of the Mass and through almsgiving, one of the three traditional practices of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and the Church teaches special care for widows and the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, render to Caesar: the coin carries Caesar's face, and every person carries God's image. Your line was you bear his image. Whose face did you see differently? Today, still in the Temple, two tiny coins. Day two hundred twenty-three.

Think of the collection basket at Mass. Some people drop in an envelope. Some tap their phone. A kid puts in a quarter his mom handed him. Nobody's watching. Or so we hope. Today, somebody is. Jesus is still in the Temple, still being questioned. Then the questions stop, and he sits down across from the treasury, where people drop their offerings into the collection chests, and he just watches. Rich people put in large amounts. And then a poor widow walks up with two coins so small they were the least money in circulation.
screen: `THE COLLECTION BASKET.` → `HE SITS AND WATCHES.` → `A WIDOW WITH TWO TINY COINS.`

segments.voice: First, the greatest commandment. Before the widow, a scribe asks Jesus which commandment is first of all. Jesus answers with the words every faithful Jew prays, then and now, the Shema. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God." Love him with your whole heart, soul, mind and strength. And the second: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The scribe agrees, and Jesus tells him: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." It's a rare warm moment between Jesus and a scribe in Mark. Second, a warning. Right after, Jesus warns about religious leaders who love long robes and the best seats, and who devour the houses of widows. Hold on to that word, widows. Third, the widow. She drops in "two mites, which make a farthing." Mites were lepta, the smallest copper coins there were. Jesus calls his disciples over: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury." The rich gave from what they had left over. She, out of her want, "cast in all she had, even her whole living." Fourth, two ways to hear it. Most Christians hear praise: whole-heart love, lived out with two coins, the commandment in action. Some readers also hear a lament, since the story sits right after the warning about those who devour widows' houses: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. The Church has usually held both. The widow is honored, and those who would take from her are warned. Either way, God measures the gift by the cost, not the amount.
screen: `THE SHEMA: LOVE WITH YOUR WHOLE HEART.` · `BEWARE THOSE WHO DEVOUR WIDOWS' HOUSES.` · `TWO MITES, MORE THAN ALL.` · `MEASURED BY COST, NOT AMOUNT.` · then, large: `SHE OF HER WANT CAST IN ALL SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something small that costs. Settle and breathe. Ask yourself: what would be a two-coin gift for me today? Not a big donation. Something small that you'll actually feel. Your lunch hour, for someone who needs to talk. The last of the good coffee. A few dollars you were saving for yourself. An apology that costs your pride. Pick one. Picture giving it. Notice the little pinch. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
The widow's two mites. Two of the smallest coins there were, and Jesus says she gave more than all the rich, because she gave all she had. Today's word.
Your line: all she had. Today, give your small costly thing, and don't tell anyone how much it cost you. Day two hundred twenty-three.

224.title: Watch (Mark 13)
224.hook: the Temple will fall, no one knows the hour, so watch
224.howItsDone: Catholics hear Jesus's call to watch at the start of Advent each year, and profess in the Creed that Christ will come again, while the Church teaches that no one can know the day or the hour.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the widow's two mites: she gave more than all the rich, because she gave all she had. Your line was all she had. What small thing did it cost you? Today they leave the Temple, and the week ends with one word. Day two hundred twenty-four.

Picture a small-town fisherman seeing a great city for the first time. As they walk out of the Temple, one of the disciples can't help himself: Master, look at these stones! Look at these buildings! And they were enormous, some of the biggest cut stones in the ancient world, gleaming on the hill. Jesus looks at them and says every stone will be thrown down. Then he climbs the Mount of Olives, sits facing the Temple, and four of the disciples ask him quietly: when? What happens next is the longest speech Jesus gives in all of Mark.
screen: `LOOK AT THESE STONES!` → `EVERY STONE THROWN DOWN.` → `WHEN? THE LONGEST SPEECH IN MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the stones. In the Douay-Rheims: "There shall not be left a stone upon a stone, that shall not be thrown down." About forty years later, in the year 70, Roman armies crushed a revolt and burned the Temple. For Mark's first readers, this may have been very recent news. Second, the troubles. Jesus speaks of wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes, famines, false messiahs, families divided, persecution. It's hard to hear. But he keeps saying: don't be alarmed. The end is not yet. Hold on. Third, the surprise. After all those signs, he says something almost no one expects: "But of that day or hour no man knoweth, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father." Nobody gets a date. Not the angels. Not even the Son. Christians have argued for centuries about what it means that the Son doesn't know; the Church has read it in light of his true humanity, and of what was his to reveal. What's certain is this: anyone who sets a date for the end of the world is going against this verse. Fourth, the doorkeeper. Jesus ends with a picture: a man goes on a journey and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake, because the master might come back in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Some readers notice those four times come back in the next chapters: the supper in the evening, the garden at night, Peter at cockcrow, Pilate in the morning. And the last line of the speech: "And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch." This week in Mark: the children, the rich man, Bartimaeus, the fig tree, Caesar's coin, the widow. And now, one word for everyone.
screen: `NOT A STONE UPON A STONE.` · `THE END IS NOT YET.` · `NO ONE KNOWS THE DAY OR HOUR.` · `THE DOORKEEPER STAYS AWAKE.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY TO YOU, I SAY TO ALL: WATCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish today as if it matters. Settle and breathe. Watching doesn't mean staring at the sky or reading the news in a panic. It means being awake to what's in front of you. Think through the rest of today. One unfinished thing you've been putting off. One person you haven't really paid attention to. Choose one, and decide to finish it, or face them, before you sleep. If you pray, you can offer the rest of the day. The bell holds the time.
Watch. The last word of Jesus's longest speech in Mark: stay awake, because no one knows the hour. Today's word.
Your line: watch. Today, three times, stop and ask: am I awake right now, or on autopilot? Then do the next thing awake. Day two hundred twenty-four.
